title: Sudan's long war
dek: Since 15 April 2023, fighting between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has killed at least 59,000 people by one count, and possibly far more, and driven about 13 million from their homes. Both sides deny targeting civilians. The war now reaches into Abyei and South Sudan.

story.text: The war broke out in Khartoum on 15 April 2023, after the army and the Rapid Support Forces split over plans to fold the paramilitary into the military. The conflict monitor ACLED has recorded at least 59,000 deaths in three years and says the real toll is likely higher; in 2024 the US envoy cited estimates of up to 150,000. Both sides now use armed drones: the UN human rights office recorded more than 1,000 civilians killed by drone strikes between January and May 2026.
story.takeaway: The war began in Khartoum on 15 April 2023. ACLED has recorded at least 59,000 deaths and says the real toll is likely higher.

story.text: In Darfur, the RSF and allied militias besieged El Fasher for more than 18 months and overran it on 26 October 2025. The UN human rights office says more than 6,000 people were killed in just over three days: at least 4,400 inside the city and more than 1,600 as they fled. It says the real toll is “undoubtedly significantly higher” and that sexual violence was used systematically as a weapon of war.
story.takeaway: When the RSF overran El Fasher in October 2025, the UN says more than 6,000 people were killed in just over three days.

visual.title: People killed in El Fasher in just over three days (UN human rights office)

story.text: The war crosses borders. On Monday 19 October 2026 a drone strike on Amiet Market in Abyei, an area claimed by both Sudan and South Sudan, killed at least 153 people, a local official says. South Sudan blames Sudan's army; an unnamed Sudanese officer told AP the army hit fuel tankers bound for the RSF. In November 2025 an RSF drone attack on the Heglig oil facility halted production and exports in parts of Sudan and South Sudan, where oil brings in more than 90% of government revenue.

About 13 million people have been forced from their homes; UNHCR says 4.3 million are refugees in neighbouring countries, most in Egypt and eastern Chad. Famine was confirmed in Zamzam camp in 2024 and in El Fasher and Kadugli in 2025. In May 2026 the IPC found no area in famine but 14 areas at risk, and nearly 19.5 million people, more than 40% of the population, facing high levels of acute food insecurity.
story.takeaway: About 13 million people have been forced from their homes; 4.3 million are refugees abroad.

story.text: Both sides face accusations. In January 2025 the US found that the RSF was committing genocide; in 2025 it also found that Sudan's government had used chemical weapons in 2024, which Sudan denies. The International Criminal Court says it has “concrete evidence” linking RSF leaders to recent war crimes in Darfur. UN-led talks on a ceasefire resumed in Geneva in October 2026 without either warring party at the table.
story.figcap: US genocide finding on the RSF
story.takeaway: Both sides face accusations of atrocities, and ceasefire talks resumed without either warring party.

story.text: Drone strikes are intensifying. On 25 October the UN human rights office said strikes attributed to both the army and the RSF killed at least 306 people in the first three weeks of October 2026. The deadliest it listed hit a transport truck at Dibab, West Kordofan, on 18 October, killing at least 139. UN rights chief Volker Türk said drones have caused most of Sudan's conflict-related civilian deaths this year.

On the evening of 26 October a drone strike hit a busy market in west Nyala, South Darfur, which the RSF holds. MSF, which attributes it to the Sudanese Armed Forces, said Nyala Teaching Hospital received 36 bodies, 21 in civilian clothing, and more than 150 wounded; the rights group Emergency Lawyers put the toll above 100. The army has not commented. On 27 October large parts of Khartoum lost power for over 12 hours after a drone hit a transformer station in Omdurman; an electricity official blamed the RSF.

On 29 October UNICEF said at least five children, three boys and two girls aged 7 to 14, were among those killed in the Nyala market strike. The same day a Yale Humanitarian Research Lab report, based on satellite imagery, found a near-total absence of civilian life in El Fasher a year after the RSF took the city, with excavation and burning sites at five hospitals and an earth barrier about 75 km around it. The report says this contradicts RSF claims that life has returned to normal.

On 30 October Al Jazeera reported an investigation by the Centre for Information Resilience, a UK open-source group, which identifies 25 commanders of the RSF, the Sudanese Armed Forces and allied forces it has reasonable grounds to believe were directly or indirectly responsible for sexual violence at five locations and periods of reported abuse, including El Fasher, Zamzam camp and parts of Gezira. The group does not attribute specific rapes to individuals. Neither force responded to Al Jazeera; both have previously denied sexual violence by their personnel.

On 31 October UN Secretary-General António Guterres, through his spokesman, said he "strongly condemns the escalating drone attacks in Sudan by the parties to the conflict" and called for civilians and civilian infrastructure to be spared, AFP reports. The statement followed the 26 October strike on Nyala's Tanqonj market, which AFP says killed at least 102 people and which has been attributed to the army. No army or RSF response was reported.

On 1 November displaced people in Blue Nile state told Radio Tamazuj that aid was not meeting their basic needs, with food and medicines short and mosquito-borne disease spreading. The state's humanitarian aid commissioner, Gisma Abdel-Karim, put the displaced at about 27,400 (Dabanga, citing the commission on 28 October, gives the figure as families, in three localities) and said WFP, ADRA and Islamic Relief were delivering food baskets, cash and hygiene supplies. Fighting in the state involves the army, the RSF and the SPLM's armed wing, Dabanga reports.

On 2 November drones struck the New Halfa and Aroma substations in Kassala state and the Al-Ghazali substation near Merowe, cutting electricity across Merowe and much of Kassala; Abu Hamad and Al-Dabbah substations were hit the day before. At least 16 power stations were targeted in a week across seven states, Anadolu reports. Sudan's government filed complaints with the UN Security Council and the African Union accusing Ethiopia of involvement in attacks on civilian infrastructure; Ethiopia had no immediate comment. Sudanese authorities and rights groups accuse the RSF of targeting infrastructure; the RSF generally does not comment and says it protects civilians.

On 2 November CPJ called on Sudan to repeal a 19 October amendment to Article 51(a) of the 1991 Criminal Act, on "waging war against the state", which makes showing support through online or media posts for actions threatening state security illegal; CPJ says journalists could face life in prison or the death penalty. The Sudanese Journalists Syndicate warned it could be used to prosecute journalists and encourage self-censorship. The army did not respond to CPJ.

Drone strikes killed at least 14 civilians on 2–3 November, residents and local sources told Radio Dabanga: eight in Um Dibo, El Sunut locality, West Kordofan, on Monday evening; at least four, with more than 10 injured, when a drone hit a fuel station in El Abbasiya Tagali market, South Kordofan, on Tuesday; and a woman and a young man in Ed Damazin, Blue Nile, on Tuesday evening. The Blue Nile Civil Society Initiative blamed the RSF and its ally, the SPLM-North, for the Ed Damazin strikes; the state governor condemned them. No RSF response was reported. The Arab League said strikes it attributed to the RSF on power stations could amount to a war crime.

On 6 November the UN refugee agency and the International Organization for Migration said 15.4 million people in Sudan urgently need emergency shelter, but funding lets agencies prioritise only about 10% of them; 936,000 have received help so far. "Our warehouses are completely empty now," IOM's Sudan chief Mohamed Refaat said.

On 7 November residents of Damazin, capital of Blue Nile region, told Radio Tamazuj that power, water and grain mills had been disrupted and that some families had fled, amid fighting in Kurmuk, Geissan and Wad al-Mahi localities and reports of RSF and SPLM-N advances. One resident said the city was calm and urged people to ignore rumours; no official statement was reported.

On 8 November Sudan's military detained Ahmed Haroun, chairman of the former ruling National Congress Party, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court over alleged crimes against humanity and war crimes in Darfur, two defence lawyers told AP; they said he was held in Kassala and his whereabouts were unknown, while a party official told Radio Tamazuj he was held by military intelligence in Khartoum. Held since 2019, he walked out of prison after it was attacked during the war, AP reports; the military had declined to hand him to the ICC, and he denies the charges. The Emergency Lawyers group has called for his handover. There was no immediate comment from the army or the ICC.

On 10 November UNICEF spokesperson James Elder said two in three child casualties in Sudan this year were caused by armed drones, and that up to 15 power stations were hit in October, cutting water and other services. UNICEF said it could not determine who carried out the strikes on power stations; no army or RSF comment was reported.

official.text: Army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan rejects negotiations and says the “military option” will continue until the RSF is removed from Sudan. The RSF has repeatedly denied widespread killings in Darfur; its leader, Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, has acknowledged abuses by his fighters but disputed their scale, and the RSF and its allies have formed a parallel government in areas they hold. The RSF did not respond to AP's request for comment on the UN's El Fasher findings. Asked about the Centre for Information Resilience's findings on sexual violence, neither the RSF nor the army responded to Al Jazeera; both have previously denied such abuses. Sudan's government accuses Ethiopia of involvement in drone attacks on infrastructure; Ethiopia had no immediate comment, and the RSF generally does not comment. The army did not respond to CPJ about the Article 51 amendment.

The RSF has repeatedly denied widespread killings in Darfur; its leader, Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, has acknowledged abuses by his fighters but disputed their scale.
The RSF and its allies have formed a parallel government in areas they hold.
The RSF did not respond to AP's request for comment on the UN's El Fasher findings.
Neither the RSF nor the army responded to Al Jazeera on the sexual-violence findings; both have previously denied such abuses.

whats_new.text: UNICEF says two in three child casualties in Sudan this year were caused by armed drones, and up to 15 power stations were hit in October. It could not say who launched them; neither side commented.

summary.label: What's happening
summary.text: Since April 2023 Sudan's army and the paramilitary RSF have fought a war that has killed at least 59,000 people by one count.

summary.label: Why it matters
summary.text: About 13 million people have fled their homes, and the UN rights chief says drones have caused most civilian deaths this year.

summary.label: What's next
summary.text: UN-led ceasefire talks resumed in Geneva in October without either side; the army chief rejects negotiations.
